entries.title: retribution and malice

entries.content:
I just finished the Complete Ghost Stories of M. R. James — the first time, I think, I’ve read them all in one go, though over the years I’ve read most of them several times.  

James calls them “ghost stories,” though as far as I can tell only one of them (“A Neighbour’s Landmark”) features a ghost — if we distinguish, as I think we should, a ghost (a disembodied though possibly visible dead person) from a revenant (a reanimated corpse). In James the revenant is the norm, along with demons, which usually bear some kind of half-human half-animal appearance, like the creatures in The Island of Doctor Moreau (which I wonder if James knew).

As Adam Roberts writes in a forthcoming review of a new James biography, “there’s rarely anything spectral or evanescent about James’s hauntings: they almost always possess a hideous physicality, a solidity, palpability and presence.” Precisely. A great many fearful things in James’s stories are hairy, and most of them have mouths. And consider this moment from “The Treasure of Abbot Thomas,” in which the narrator is striving to discover the hidden treasure of the title:

Well, I felt to the right, and my fingers touched something curved, that felt — yes — more or less like leather; dampish it was, and evidently part of a heavy, full thing. There was nothing, I must say, to alarm one. I grew bolder, and putting both hands in as well as I could, I pulled it to me, and it came. It was heavy, but moved more easily than I had expected…. Then I heard [an assistant] call softly, “All right, sir,” and went on pulling out the great bag, in complete darkness. It hung for an instant on the edge of the hole, then slipped forward on to my chest, and put its arms round my neck.

Yeeeeeesh.

In an essay about writing ghost stories, James says that the two major forms that threat takes in his stories are retribution and malice. Most of the people to whom bad things happen in his stories deserve it — they receive retribution for their sins and crimes — but some are just unlucky in running across malicious things.

The chief topoi, as it were, of the stories are

  • the Vengeful Dead
  • Demonic Guardians
  • Cursed Objects
  • Flight and Pursuit
  • Prophetic Dreams

The Cursed Objects are typically either books (linked to the lust for forbidden knowledge) or treasure (linked to greed). James seems especially compelled by stories of people fleeing, almost always ineffectually, from some horror. Probably the most powerful example comes from the most famous story, “‘Oh, Whistle, and I’ll come to You, My Lad,’“ which I think I can quote here without ruining the whole story. The narrator is having a Prophetic Dream:

A long stretch of shore — shingle edged by sand, and intersected at short intervals with black groynes running down to the water — a scene, in fact, so like that of his afternoon’s walk that, in the absence of any landmark, it could not be distinguished therefrom. The light was obscure, conveying an impression of gathering storm, late winter evening, and slight cold rain. On this bleak stage at first no actor was visible. Then, in the distance, a bobbing black object appeared; a moment more, and it was a man running, jumping, clambering over the groynes, and every few seconds looking eagerly back. The nearer he came the more obvious it was that he was not only anxious, but even terribly frightened, though his face was not to be distinguished. He was, moreover, almost at the end of his strength. On he came; each successive obstacle seemed to cause him more difficulty than the last. ‘Will he get over this next one?’ thought Parkins; ‘it seems a little higher than the others.’ Yes; half climbing, half throwing himself, he did get over, and fell all in a heap on the other side (the side nearest to the spectator). There, as if really unable to get up again, he remained crouching under the groyne, looking up in an attitude of painful anxiety.

So far no cause whatever for the fear of the runner had been shown; but now there began to be seen, far up the shore, a little flicker of something light-coloured moving to and fro with great swiftness and irregularity. Rapidly growing larger, it, too, declared itself as a figure in pale, fluttering draperies, ill-defined. There was something about its motion which made Parkins very unwilling to see it at close quarters. It would stop, raise arms, bow itself toward the sand, then run stooping across the beach to the water-edge and back again; and then, rising upright, once more continue its course forward at a speed that was startling and terrifying. The moment came when the pursuer was hovering about from left to right only a few yards beyond the groyne where the runner lay in hiding. After two or three ineffectual castings hither and thither it came to a stop, stood upright, with arms raised high, and then darted straight forward towards the groyne.

Once more I say: Yeeeeeesh.

Demons and the Vengeful Dead never (to my recollection) appear in a single story: the norm is just one of them as the primary danger. But otherwise the elements may appear in any combination.

What is extraordinary about the stories is how much variety of interest and imagination James is able to sustain — at least until late in his career: the final stories are brief and uninspired — from this extremely limited palette of options. These things are so foundational to the human experience of dread that they are capable, it appears, of being recombined infinitely. Endless forms most terrible and most dreadful, to rewrite Darwin.

entries.content:
Steven Spielberg’s Munich (2005), we’re told, is “based on real events” but that should probably read “very loosely based on real events.” That was relatively clear when the movie was released but has become incontrovertible as time has gone by. I don’t want to get into any of that, though; indeed, I don’t want to get into anything about this mediocre film — except its last scene, which is fascinating. So, obviously, spoilers ahead. 

Avner (Eric Bana) has been an assassin in a deep-undercover mission for Mossad. He has killed several Palestinians who had been named to him as participants in the 1972 killing of Israeli Olympians in Munich; he has come to question the morality of his job, and has left Mossad and moved with his wife and child to Brooklyn. But this move has not brought the peace he had hoped for: he thinks he is being watched and that his family is in danger. He goes in a rage to the Israeli consulate, from which he is forcibly removed. Soon thereafter he gets a visit from his former minder, Ephraim (Geoffrey Rush, in the film’s best performance). Ephraim tells Avner that he and his family are in no danger, and that the people Avner killed really were murderers — but the main thing he wants to do is this: plead for Avner to return to Israel. He doesn’t belong in America; he belongs in his homeland — he is a sabra, born in Israel, raised in a kibbutz. He owes everything to Israel. (The whole point of Israel, David Ben-Gurion always said, was to give the world’s Jews a home to come to — thus the Chok HaShvut, the Law of Return.) For a sabra to leave Israel is, in Ephraim’s eyes, both an unnatural act and a betrayal. 

To this plea Avner responds with the beginnings of a shake of the head, a gestural No — but he arrests that movement. Instead he says, “Come to my house for dinner tonight. Come on, you’re a Jew, you’re a stranger. It’s written somewhere that I should invite you to break bread with me. So, break bread with me, Ephraim.” Ephraim is a stranger (ger) in New York City, a phrasing which strongly suggests that Avner is not a stranger there, that he has made a home there. Like Abraham in Genesis 18, Avner is practicing hachnasat orchim, the welcoming of gerim. It is one of the essential mitzvot. But it seems to me also that by suggesting this meeting, Avner is deferring his refusal; he is giving Ephraim a chance to persuade him.

The historical context here is vital. In the aftermath of the Yom Kippur War in 1973, a number of Israelis, feeling that their country would never be safe, decided to leave. The coming of the world’s Jews to Israel was commonly called aliyah, or “ascent”; departure from Israel came to be called yerida, “descent,” and those who depart named yordim. In 1976, the Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin spoke of the yordim with utter contempt, calling them nefolet shel nemushot — a metaphor from the harvesting of wheat that means something like “the leftovers of the weaklings,” the rejects of the rejects. The worst of the worst. It’s worth noting that this meeting between Avner and Ephraim occurs right around the time of Rabin’s statement and the controversy it caused in Israel. Though Ephram doesn’t use the phrase, he clearly thinks that Avner is among the nefolet shel nemushot — he is weak, he is worthless. Ephraim has no bond with such a person. 

After Avner extends his invitation, Ephraim looks at him for a moment, then says simply: “No.” And he walks away.

P.S. The controversy over yerida has continued. I just learned about this: 

In 2011, Israel’s Ministry of Immigrant Absorption created a now-infamous ad campaign, hoping to guilt Israelis abroad into coming home. In one of the ads, a little boy, done with coloring, turns to his father. But Dad is asleep in an easy chair, an Economist draped over his chest. “Daddy?” the boy calls, to no avail. A pause. He tries again, this time in a whisper: “Abba?” Dad’s eyes open at once. The artwork is admired; hair is affectionately ruffled. The scene fades, and a narrator says in Hebrew: “They will always remain Israelis. Their children won’t. Help them return to the land.”

entries.title: four big books
entries.summary: Four Big Books is the title of a course I’ll be teaching this coming term — my last as a university professor! What follows is an outline of what I’ll be saying to my student on the first day of class. • • • • • Back in 1982, at the Cannes Film Festival, the […]
entries.content:
Four Big Books is the title of a course I’ll be teaching this coming term — my last as a university professor! What follows is an outline of what I’ll be saying to my student on the first day of class.

• • • • •

Back in 1982, at the Cannes Film Festival, the German film director Wim Wenders brought other filmmakers, one by one, to a hotel room so that he might film them answering a series of questions he had written, all of which gathered like iron shavings around a single magnetic question: Is cinema dying? The resulting film, Room 666, is generally fascinating, but now seems an exercise from another world, since the primary threat to cinema then was television. Things have changed. Forty years later Lubna Playoust repeated the exercise, with many more filmmakers and Wenders himself: thus Room 999.

One of the most interesting reflections in Room 999 comes from the French filmmaker and writer Audrey Diwan. Diwan is the mother of teenage children who (she suggests) spend a lot of time on Instagram, and as she watched one particular Reel she asked herself: What is the appeal of this? The feature films she makes might be described as seeking to identify meaning in experience, or maybe just to provide entertainment, but Reels, she thinks, don’t do either of these things. When she asked her children what they like about these very short videos, they told her that they find them satisfying. (Diwan speaks in French, but “satisfaction” is the same in that language and in English.) Even though videos so short can only provide “crumbs of narrative,” nevertheless, “to them, it’s a few seconds of intense satisfaction.” And they prefer this satisfaction to whatever rewards might come from the movies that Diwan makes, or the older movies that mean the most to her, the ones that made her want to be a filmmaker. Her children can’t adjust to the rhythm and pace of movies: “They no longer tolerate the notion of time passing.”

At this point Diwan goes into who-am-I-to-judge mode, saying that she’s just “an old person” — she was 41 at the time of the interview — who, like all old persons, must acknowledge that “at some point, you stop feeling that the world is yours.” But nevertheless, she thinks of her children: “I wonder how they’ll orchestrate their own narratives.” So for her the most fundamental issue raised by Wim Wenders all those decades ago concerns not cinema as such, but rather the fate of “stories and storytelling.” She asks: “What will become of cinema if we have no grasp of time?” But the greater question, only implicit here: If we have no grasp of time we will have to live without narratives, without stories about ourselves or anyone and anything else — and what will that be like?

No human life offers, or ever can offer, the particular “satisfaction” — the near-instantaneous closure — of a Reel or a TikTok; but to make of your life anything more than a succession of unrelated momentary experiences requires some “grasp of time.” The identifying and unfolding of a pattern over time, perhaps over many years, is one of the key purposes of art — not the only one, but a central and essential one. In some cases a full apprehension of pattern may be possible, as when Czesław Miłosz remembers himself as a child: “he knew what was needed for some ultimate moment / When he would compose from fragments a world perfect at last.” In other cases the pattern remains inscrutable, indiscernible: “On Margate Sands. I can connect nothing with nothing” — and when that happens, it is the function of art to record the experience and make it vivid. After all, all of us have times when we can connect nothing with nothing, and can only hope that a pattern will eventually emerge: “The tight place, the dark pit in which I am now lying, of what bird is it the talon? When the design of my life is complete, shall I, shall other people see a stork?”

A few hundred years ago, a particular form of art arose that would eventually prove the most lasting and powerful means by which ordinary people, especially but not only in the Western world, discern and reflect on the patterns of their lives. This form is called the novel, and almost from the beginning it was clear that the most ambitious and serious of novels needed to be quite long. Though there are many powerful short novels, they tend not to strive for the kind of comprehensiveness — describing people behaviorally and psychologically, yes, but also embedding them in their full social contexts, sometimes over the course of several generations — that the very greatest novels pursue.

When Audrey Diwan speaks of “orchestrating” one’s narrative, the term is especially appropriate to these Big Books: they are orchestral in their sweep and scope, in their changes of tempo and mood, and perhaps above all in the number of distinct instruments they employ. But while a great symphony can be experienced in less than an hour, a big novel takes many, many hours to read. That’s because big novels are especially concerned to immerse us in the medium of time.

In this class, I am asking you to read four large, ambitious, comprehensive novels that test our patience, our determination, our memory — but that also offer some of the greatest rewards that art can offer. They are:

  • Honoré de Balzac, Lost Illusions (1843)
  • George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans), Middlemarch (1872)
  • Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878)
  • Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880)

The dates I have given here are the dates of complete book publication, but the first readers of these novels didn’t read them as books: they read them in installments. Lost Illusions was published over the course of six years, the first part as a stand-alone book, the rest in magazines. Middlemarch was published as eight small books over the course of a year. Each of the two Russian novels was published a chunk at a time over the course of many months in a periodical called The Russian Messenger. People had time — for many of them, far too much time! — to reflect on each installment and long for the next one to appear.

We’re going to move faster than the original pace of publication — presumably nobody wants to be in this class in 2028 – but slower than is usual in college classrooms where novels are read. We’re going to live with these characters in ways not too unlike the ways the books’ first readers did … and we’re also going to spend a good deal of time reflecting on the value of this kind of experience in our age of microvideos. Do great big novels offer a different kind of satisfaction than Audrey Diwan’s children get from their Reels? Or do they offer something altogether other?

And one more thing. We may not all be Christians in this room, but most of us are, and one of the most common features of the Christian life, as of the Jewish life, is the struggle to discern a pattern. Just read the Psalms if you don’t believe me: think of how the Psalmist in times of blessing recalls times of misery, in times of misery recalls times of blessing. What does it all add up to, though? What’s the essential shape of the story? Does the Lord really have His hand on my life? No Reel can tell.
